title: Routing with React Router
summary: Routing chooses which page part to show for a web address.
introduction: Routing chooses which page part to show for a web address. Think of a school map that points to different rooms. Use React Router to connect an address to a page and add links between pages.
learningObjectives: Install React Router and wrap the app in a BrowserRouter
Declare routes with Routes and Route and link between them
Read dynamic URL segments with useParams
Share a layout between pages with nested routes and Outlet

blocks.text: Without a router, every page is the same `App` and the URL never changes. That breaks bookmarks, sharing, the back button and search engines. A router keeps the URL and the rendered component tree in sync: changing one changes the other, using the browser's History API instead of a page load.

React Router 7 ships as the single `react-router` package; `react-router-dom` still exists as a re-export for older imports, so both names work, but new code imports from `react-router`. Wrap the application in `BrowserRouter` once, in `main.jsx`:

blocks.title: src/main.jsx

blocks.text: `BrowserRouter` listens to the URL and provides it to every routing component below it. There is also a `HashRouter` for static hosts that cannot be configured, and a `MemoryRouter` for tests.

blocks.title: src/App.jsx
Rendered at two URLs

/about →
Home About

About us

Home About

Page not found

blocks.text: `Routes` looks at the current URL, picks the best matching `Route` and renders its `element`. Matching ranks routes by how specific they are, not by declaration order, so `/about` never accidentally matches `/`. The `*` route catches everything else and is the right place for a not-found page. `Link` renders a real `<a>` tag, so middle-click and "open in new tab" work, but a normal click is intercepted and handled without a reload.

blocks.title: Common mistake: plain anchors for internal links
blocks.text: `<a href="/about">` causes a full page load: the app restarts, all state is lost and every bundle is downloaded again. Use `Link` or `NavLink` for anything inside the app and reserve `<a>` for external URLs. The other half of this mistake lives on the server: a deployed `BrowserRouter` app must serve `index.html` for every path, otherwise refreshing `/about` returns the host's 404 page.

blocks.title: ProductPage.jsx

blocks.text: A segment starting with a colon matches any value and exposes it through `useParams`, always as a **string**, so convert it with `Number` when you need arithmetic. Several segments can be dynamic (`/users/:userId/posts/:postId`). To read query strings such as `?page=2` use `useSearchParams`, which returns a `URLSearchParams` object and a setter.

Most apps share a header, navigation and footer between pages. Declare a parent route whose element is the layout, nest the page routes inside it, and render `<Outlet />` where the matched child should appear.

blocks.title: src/App.jsx with a layout

blocks.text: `NavLink` is a `Link` that knows whether it is active: it adds the `active` class and `aria-current="page"` automatically, which is all a navigation bar needs for styling and accessibility. The `end` prop stops `/` from counting as active on every page. An `index` route renders at the parent's own path.

After a successful login
blocks.content: URL: /dashboard   (the login entry is replaced in the history, so Back does not return to the form)

blocks.text: `useNavigate` returns a function for redirects after actions. `navigate(-1)` goes back, and `{ replace: true }` swaps the current history entry instead of adding one. Use `Link` for anything the user clicks and `navigate` only for programmatic transitions; links are discoverable, navigation calls are not.

questions.question: Which component renders the matched child route inside a layout route?
questions.explanation: `<Outlet />` is the placeholder in a parent route's element where the matching nested route is rendered.

questions.question: `useParams()` returns URL segment values as numbers when they look numeric.
questions.explanation: Everything in a URL is text. `useParams` always returns strings; convert with `Number(id)` when you need a number.
